clinicalPearls: Characterised by complex, formed visual hallucinations occurring in people with significant visual impairment who retain insight that the images are not real
It occurs in cognitively intact individuals without psychiatric illness and without hallucinations in other sensory modalities
Hallucinations range from simple patterns to detailed images of people, animals, faces, or scenes, sometimes with abnormal proportions
It is strongly associated with acquired vision loss, most often age-related macular degeneration, glaucoma, and diabetic retinopathy
The mechanism is thought to be release phenomena, with spontaneous activity in visually deafferented cortex generating the images
Reassurance and explanation are central to management, as many patients fear they are developing a mental illness
The retained insight distinguishes it from psychotic and delirium-related hallucinations
reference.pathophysiology: Charles Bonnet syndrome is understood as a visual release phenomenon: loss of normal visual input from ocular or anterior pathway disease leaves visual cortex deafferented, and spontaneous cortical activity in these regions is experienced as formed hallucinations, analogous to phantom sensations after limb loss. The hallucinations are purely visual, and insight is preserved because higher cognition is intact. The syndrome is most common in older people with reduced acuity from macular degeneration, glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy, or other causes of vision loss, and its prevalence rises with the severity of visual impairment.
additionalDifferentials: Visual hallucinations of Lewy body dementia or Parkinson disease
additionalInvestigations: Comprehensive ophthalmic assessment to characterise the underlying visual loss
Assessment for features of Parkinsonism or Lewy body disease
Medication review for hallucinogenic or deliriogenic drugs
Neuroimaging where atypical features or focal signs suggest a central cause
Consideration of electroencephalography if occipital seizures are suspected
redFlags: Hallucinations in other sensory modalities suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Loss of insight or delusional interpretation suggesting psychosis or delirium
Associated cognitive decline or parkinsonism suggesting a neurodegenerative disorder
Focal neurological signs suggesting a structural or epileptic cause
reference.prognosis: The syndrome is benign and hallucinations often diminish over months to years, though they may persist; the main morbidity is distress, which is greatly reduced by reassurance, and prognosis otherwise follows the underlying eye disease.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the hallucinations as psychosis or dementia and prescribing inappropriate antipsychotics
Failing to reassure the patient, who may otherwise fear mental illness
Overlooking a neurodegenerative or structural cause when atypical features are present
Not optimising the underlying visual impairment, which can worsen the hallucinations
management: Reassurance and clear explanation that the hallucinations are a release phenomenon from visual loss and not a sign of mental illness or dementia is the central intervention
Optimise the underlying eye disease to improve residual vision, including treatment of macular degeneration, cataract surgery, low-vision aids and improved lighting
Teach simple coping strategies such as blinking, shifting gaze, altering lighting and increasing social and cognitive stimulation to interrupt episodes
Review and rationalise deliriogenic or hallucinogenic medications that may aggravate symptoms
Monitor cognition and watch for parkinsonism or Lewy body features that would suggest an alternative diagnosis
Cautious trial of pharmacotherapy reserved for severe, distressing and refractory hallucinations
Referral to low-vision rehabilitation services and psychological support where distress persists
